[Migrating from Testing Library | Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/testing-library)\n\n# Playwright Component Testing for React\n\nPlaywright offers experimental component testing capabilities for React applications.[1][3] Here's what you need to know:\n\n## Getting Started\n\nInstallation is straightforward using the command:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nnpm init playwright@latest -- --ct\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis creates necessary configuration files including a &#96;playwright/index.html&#96; file (with a root div for mounting components) and test files.[1][3]\n\n## Basic Test Structure\n\nA typical component test looks like this:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';\nimport App from './App';\n\ntest('should work', async ({ mount }) =\u003e {\n  const component = await mount(\u003cApp /\u003e);\n  await expect(component).toContainText('Learn React');\n});\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRun tests with &#96;npm run test-ct&#96;.[1][3]\n\n## Key Advantages\n\nTests run in Node.js while components run in a real browser, combining the benefits of both environments.[1][3] This enables real clicks, actual layout execution, and visual regression testing while leveraging Node.js capabilities and Playwright features like parallel testing and tracing.[1][3]\n\n## Important Limitations\n\n- You can only pass plain JavaScript objects and built-in types (strings, numbers, dates) to components—not complex Node.js objects[1][3]\n- You cannot pass data synchronously through callbacks, as the callback lives in Node while the component runs in the browser[1][3]\n\n## Migration from Testing Library\n\nPlaywright provides migration guidance from React Testing Library, with equivalent APIs (e.g., &#96;render()&#96; → &#96;mount()&#96;, &#96;screen&#96; → &#96;component&#96;).[4][5]",

## Bottom Line
For your current repo, most of this list falls into 3 buckets:

- Keep using what already matches your stack: `Next.js`, `TypeScript`, `Tailwind`, `Drizzle`, `ESLint`, `Vitest`, `Playwright`, `pnpm`, `PostCSS`, `tsx`, `Node.js`, `SWC`.
- Add a small number of high-value tools soon: `Knip`, `CSpell`, `MSW`, `Sentry`, `size-limit`, and maybe `SVGO`/`SVGR`.
- Skip the rest unless your roadmap changes, because many are competing frameworks, alternate bundlers, alternate ORMs, or release/monorepo tooling you do not need for a single Next.js 16 app with its own CMS.

## Best Candidates For Your Project
If I had to shortlist the most useful additions for this specific repo, I’d pick these:

- `Knip`: best cleanup tool for unused files, exports, and dependencies.
- `CSpell`: catches bad spelling in UI text, docs, and code identifiers with very low maintenance cost.
- `Mock Service Worker`: best next testing upgrade for realistic API mocking in `Vitest` and `Playwright`.
- `Sentry`: best production monitoring upgrade once the site/admin are live.
- `size-limit`: very relevant for a public portfolio where bundle weight matters.
- `SVGO`: useful if you keep raw SVG assets.
- `SVGR`: useful if you often turn SVGs into React components.
- `simple-git-hooks` or `husky` + `lint-staged` + `commitlint`: worth it if you want stricter repo hygiene.
- `next-intl`: only if you plan multilingual content.
- `MDX` / `Next.js MDX` / `Remark`: only if you want blog posts, case studies, or richer content pages.
- `dependency-cruiser`: useful later if you want to enforce boundaries between `app`, `components`, `lib`, and admin/public areas.
- `Vercel OG`: strong fit if you want dynamic Open Graph images.

## Curated Report

- `CSpell`: `Use now`. Low-cost quality boost for UI copy, docs, and code spelling.

- `GitHub Actions`: `Use`. Same verdict as above; very relevant for this repo.
- `Mock Service Worker`: `Use soon`. Best companion to `Vitest` and `Playwright` for realistic API mocking.

- `Node.js`: `Keep`. Core runtime for Next, tooling, and CI.

Yes. A few important `Next.js 16`-relevant tools were missing from your list.

## Most Useful Missing Tools
- `@next/bundle-analyzer`
  Best missing tool for your repo. It helps you inspect client/server bundles and is very useful in a portfolio site where bundle size matters.

- `@vercel/analytics`
  Good if you deploy on Vercel and want lightweight traffic/event analytics without adding a heavier analytics stack.

- `@vercel/speed-insights`
  Very relevant for `Next.js` because it gives real Core Web Vitals and route performance data in production.

- `zod`
  This is the big one. For a `Next.js` app with forms, server actions, auth, and DB writes, `zod` is one of the most useful missing tools on the whole list.

- `next-safe-action`
  Strong fit if you lean on Server Actions. It adds typed input validation, safer execution, and cleaner action patterns on top of native Next actions.

- `react-scan`
  Very useful in development to catch unnecessary re-renders and React performance issues, especially in interactive dashboard/admin UI.

- `@axe-core/playwright`
  Excellent if you keep `Playwright`. It gives automated accessibility checks inside E2E tests and fits your public site well.

## Good Missing Tools, But More Optional
- `@vercel/og`
  You listed `Vercel OG`, which is good. If you meant the actual package/tooling layer, this is still worth calling out as a real implementation choice for dynamic OG images.

- `@next/mdx`
  You listed `MDX` and `Next.js MDX`, but the official integration package itself is worth explicitly knowing because that is what you would actually wire into the app.

- `react-hook-form`
  Not mandatory in React 19 + Server Actions, but still very useful if your admin dashboard gets larger, more dynamic forms.

- `axe-core` / `jest-axe` / `vitest-axe`
  Good companions if you want accessibility checks at unit/integration level, not only in browser E2E.

## Things I Would Not Add Despite Being Popular
- `next-seo`
  I would not treat this as a missing tool. In App Router, Next’s native metadata API already covers most SEO work better.

- `Prettier` if you move to `Biome`
  Pick one formatter direction, not both.

- `TanStack Query`
  Only add it if you have a lot of client-side async state, optimistic updates, or repeated client fetching. For a server-first `Next.js 16` app, it is not automatically needed.

## My Real Priority Order For Your Project
1. `zod`
2. `@next/bundle-analyzer`
3. `@vercel/speed-insights`
4. `@vercel/analytics`
5. `next-safe-action`
6. `@axe-core/playwright`
7. `react-scan`

Here’s what was added and how it fits your Next.js 16 stack.

## What I set up

### `prettier.config.mjs`
- Opinionated defaults aligned with typical **Next.js / TypeScript** code: **double quotes**, **semicolons**, **`trailingComma: "all"`**, **2 spaces**, **`printWidth: 100`**, **LF** line endings — see [What is Prettier?](https://prettier.io/docs/en/index.html) and [Options](https://prettier.io/docs/en/options.html).
- **`prettier-plugin-tailwindcss`** last in `plugins` so **Tailwind class lists** in `className` stay sorted (recommended for Tailwind-heavy UI).

### `.prettierignore`
- Skips **build output**, **coverage**, **reports**, **lockfiles**, **binary `public/` assets**, and **`.agents/` / `.specstory/` / `.cursor/`** so formatting stays focused on your app and stays fast.

### `package.json`
- **`format`**: `prettier --write .`
- **`format:check`**: `prettier --check .`
- Dev deps: **`prettier`**, **`prettier-plugin-tailwindcss`**, **`eslint-config-prettier`**
- Fixed the stray leading space in the **`spellcheck`** script.

### ESLint
- **`eslint-config-prettier`** is appended **after** your other configs so ESLint does **not** fight Prettier on formatting — see [Integrating with Linters](https://prettier.io/docs/en/integrating-with-linters.html).

## What you should do locally

1. Dependencies are in the lockfile from install; if needed run:  
   `pnpm install`
2. Apply formatting when you want a single baseline (you skipped the full write in this environment):  
   `pnpm format`  
   Then verify:  
   `pnpm format:check`
3. Run lint as usual:  
   `pnpm lint`

Right now **`format:check` will still report ~100 files** until you run **`pnpm format`** once; that’s expected until the codebase matches Prettier’s output.

- [Prettier documentation](https://prettier.io/docs/en/index.html)  
- [Configuration](https://prettier.io/docs/en/configuration.html)

Here’s what each **Prettier option** in your config does. (Prettier calls these **options**, not ESLint-style “rules”; they only change **formatting**, not correctness.)

## Formatting options

| Option | Value | What it does |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| **`semi`** | `true` | Inserts **semicolons** at the end of statements where JavaScript/TypeScript allows them. With `false`, Prettier would omit them (ASI style). |
| **`singleQuote`** | `false` | Uses **double quotes** (`"`) for strings in normal JS/TS. With `true`, you’d get single quotes (`'`). |
| **`jsxSingleQuote`** | `false` | In **JSX/TSX**, attribute values use **double quotes** (`className="foo"`). With `true`, JSX would use single quotes for attributes. |
| **`trailingComma`** | `"all"` | Adds **trailing commas** wherever valid in ES2017+ (objects, arrays, function params, etc.). Helps **smaller git diffs** when you add lines. `"es5"` only where ES5 allows; `"none"` removes them. |
| **`tabWidth`** | `2` | Treats one **indentation level** as **2 spaces** when breaking lines (e.g. wrapped function args, nested blocks). |
| **`useTabs`** | `false` | **Spaces** are used for indentation. With `true`, Prettier would indent with **tab characters** (width still influenced by `tabWidth` for alignment in some cases). |
| **`printWidth`** | `100` | Soft wrap target: Prettier tries to keep lines **up to ~100 characters** before wrapping. Not a hard limit for long strings; it’s a preference for when to break. |
| **`bracketSpacing`** | `true` | In object literals, **spaces inside `{}`**: `{ foo: 1 }`. With `false`: `{foo: 1}`. |
| **`bracketSameLine`** | `false` | For JSX, the **`>`** of a multiline opening tag goes on **its own line** before children (classic React style). With `true`, the `>` would stay on the same line as the last attribute. |
| **`arrowParens`** | `"always"` | Arrow functions always get **parens around a single argument**: `(x) => x`. With `"as-needed"`, you’d get `x => x` when possible. |
| **`endOfLine`** | `"lf"` | Line endings are **LF** (`\n`), normal for Linux/macOS and typical for Git repos. Alternatives: `"crlf"` (Windows), `"auto"` (keep existing). |

## Plugins (not formatting style)

| Key | Value | What it does |
|-----|--------|----------------|
| **`plugins`** | `["prettier-plugin-tailwindcss"]` | Loads the **Tailwind Prettier plugin**. It **sorts/classifies** utility classes inside `className` strings (and similar) in a consistent order. It must stay **last** in the array if you add other Prettier plugins later. |

Official reference for all of these: [Prettier options](https://prettier.io/docs/en/options.html).

## `singleQuote` and `jsxSingleQuote`

There is **no objectively better** choice. It is team/style consistency.

- **`singleQuote: true`** — `'hello'` in JS/TS. Common in many codebases; slightly fewer keystrokes; pairs naturally with double-quoted JSX attributes if you use **`jsxSingleQuote: false`** (strings in code vs markup look different).
- **`singleQuote: false`** (your config) — `"hello"`. Very common in TS/React; matches JSON and many style guides; easy to read in templates.

**`jsxSingleQuote`** only affects **JSX/TSX attribute quotes**:

- **`jsxSingleQuote: false`** — `className="btn"` (typical React docs style).
- **`jsxSingleQuote: true`** — `className='btn'`. Fine if you want single quotes in markup only.

Many teams use **`singleQuote: true`** + **`jsxSingleQuote: false`** so normal code uses `'` and JSX still looks like most tutorials. Your setup (**double everywhere**) is equally valid and very consistent.

---

## How many spaces is “one tab”?

In **your** config:

- **`useTabs: false`** — Prettier does **not** emit tab characters for indentation. It uses **spaces**. **`tabWidth: 2`** means **each indent level is 2 spaces** (nested block = 4, 6, …).

If you set **`useTabs: true`**, “one tab” is **one tab character** (`\t`). Then **`tabWidth`** is mainly used for **alignment** and how wide editors treat a tab for layout (often still shown as 2 or 4 “columns”). So: **with spaces, “tab” in the sense of “one indent” = `tabWidth` spaces (here, 2). With real tabs, one indent = one `\t`.**

---

## `bracketSameLine` — examples

This only matters when a **JSX opening tag is split across multiple lines** (many attributes or long lines).

**`bracketSameLine: false`** (your setting, classic style) — the closing **`>`** of the opening tag is on its **own line**:

```tsx
<button
  type="submit"
  className="px-4 py-2"
>
  Save
</button>
```

**`bracketSameLine: true`** — the **`>`** stays on the **same line as the last attribute**:

```tsx
<button
  type="submit"
  className="px-4 py-2">
  Save
</button>
```

Same idea for components with children: `false` puts `>` alone on a line before children; `true` keeps `>` right after the last prop line. Pick what you find readable; Prettier’s default has varied over time—**`false`** is still a very common React style.

---

## “Best” `arrowParens`

Not objective either.

- **`"always"`** — `(x) => x`, `(a, b) => a + b`. Always parentheses for single-arg arrows. **Pros:** stable when you add a second parameter or a type annotation; fewer noisy diffs. **Cons:** slightly more characters.
- **`"as-needed"`** — `x => x` when there’s only one simple param. **Pros:** shorter. **Cons:** changing the parameter list can reformat more.

For **TypeScript**, many teams prefer **`"always"`** because typed single params like `(id: string) =>` already need parens. **`"always"`** is a safe default.

---

## Purpose of `endOfLine`

It controls **line endings** in files Prettier writes:

- **`"lf"`** — Unix/macOS style (`\n`). Normal for Linux servers, Docker, most CI, and Git on Unix.
- **`"crlf"`** — Windows style (`\r\n`). Some Windows-only tooling expects it.
- **`"auto"`** — keep what’s already in the file (less consistent across clones).

**Why it matters:** mixing LF and CRLF causes noisy diffs and sometimes “whole file changed” in Git. Teams usually pick **one** (often **`lf`**) and align **Git** (e.g. `core.autocrlf`) or **`.gitattributes`** so everyone gets the same endings. Your **`lf`** is a solid default for a Node/Next app on modern hosting.

## What Prettier does to `.md` files

You **do not need a Prettier plugin** for normal **Markdown** (`.md`). Prettier ships with a **built-in Markdown parser** and will format those files when they are not ignored (e.g. by `.prettierignore`).

Roughly, it will:

- **Normalize whitespace** around headings, lists, block quotes, and horizontal rules (within its rules).
- **Format fenced code blocks** by running the right inner formatter when it knows the language (e.g. JS, JSON, CSS).
- **Respect / reflow prose** depending on **`proseWrap`** (see below).
- **Handle GFM-style tables** (alignment, spacing) where supported by its parser.

So for “make my markdown prettier and consistent,” **Prettier alone is enough** in most repos.

## Option that matters most: `proseWrap`

Prettier’s behavior on **paragraph text** is controlled by **`proseWrap`** ([docs](https://prettier.io/docs/en/options.html#prose-wrap)):

| Value | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| **`"preserve"`** (common default for Markdown) | Keeps your **manual line breaks** in paragraphs. Safer for docs that rely on “one line per sentence” or Git-friendly diffs. |
| **`"always"`** | Wraps prose to **`printWidth`** (with your config, 100 columns). Can create **large diffs** in long `.md` files. |
| **`"never"`** | Avoids wrapping prose in a way that reflows lines (paragraphs tend to stay on fewer long lines). |

You didn’t set `proseWrap` in `prettier.config.mts`, so Prettier uses its **default** for Markdown (currently **`preserve`** in recent Prettier versions). If you want hard-wrapped readme-style lines at 100 chars, set `proseWrap: "always"` in config (often with an **`overrides`** block only for `*.md` so code files are unchanged).

## Do you need anything else for Markdown?

| Need | Tool |
|------|------|
| **Formatting only** | **Prettier** (no extra Prettier plugin for plain `.md`). |
| **Linting** (heading levels, duplicate headings, list style, etc.) | **`markdownlint`** (CLI or editor) — **not** Prettier; it checks rules, it doesn’t replace Prettier. |
| **`.mdx`** (Markdown + JSX) | Prettier can format **`.mdx`** with its **MDX** support; very complex MDX sometimes needs care, but you still usually **don’t** add a separate Prettier plugin for basic MDX. |
| **Custom doc pipeline** (remark/rehype plugins, Astro/Starlight, etc.) | That’s **separate** from Prettier; use your framework’s toolchain; Prettier doesn’t run your full remark plugin stack. |

## Your repo specifically

- **`prettier-plugin-tailwindcss`** only affects files/locations where Tailwind class strings are handled (e.g. HTML/JSX `class`/`className`). It does **not** replace a Markdown formatter for normal prose `.md` files.
- If `.md` is listed in **`.prettierignore`**, Prettier will **skip** those paths entirely — worth checking if docs never seem to format.

**Summary:** For `.md`, Prettier is enough for formatting; add **`markdownlint`** (or similar) only if you want **lint rules**, and tune **`proseWrap`** if you care how paragraphs wrap vs stay as you typed them.

_**Agent (composer-2-fast)**_


Here’s how Prettier uses them for **Markdown** (and similar prose):

## `proseWrap: "preserve"`

- **Keeps the line breaks you already have** inside a paragraph (and generally avoids reflowing prose to `printWidth`).
- Good when **line breaks matter** for you (diffs, “one sentence per line,” or tools that care about how lines are split).

**Example:** If your source has two lines in one paragraph:

```md
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit.
Curabitur consectetur maximus risus.
```

Prettier will **not** glue those into one wrapped block (it **preserves** that structure).

---

## `proseWrap: "never"`

- **Does not wrap** prose to `printWidth`.
- For paragraph text, it tends to **collapse** inner line breaks so each paragraph becomes **one long line** (until the next blank line), instead of keeping your manual breaks.

So the practical difference vs **`preserve`**:  
**`never`** = “don’t wrap to column width” and often **unwraps** lines in a paragraph into a single line.  
**`preserve`** = “don’t reflow for width; **keep** the author’s line breaks.”

---

## Compared to `"always"`

- **`"always"`** reflows paragraph text so lines fit **`printWidth`** (e.g. 100 columns). That’s the one that **hard-wraps** prose.

---

**Rule of thumb**

- Want **manual line breaks kept** → **`preserve`** (also the usual default for Markdown in Prettier).
- Want **each paragraph as one long line** (no manual mid-paragraph breaks) → closer to **`never`** behavior, but read the [official `proseWrap` docs](https://prettier.io/docs/en/options.html#prose-wrap) for your Prettier version because wording and edge cases are refined over time.

The distinction is also discussed in [this Prettier issue](https://github.com/prettier/prettier/issues/6488) about `never` vs `preserve`.
